posts.title: Multi-agent is a routing problem
posts.hook: Everyone's excited about multi-agent orchestration. Almost nobody is talking about the boring part that actually matters.
posts.body:
Everyone's excited about multi-agent orchestration. Almost nobody is talking about the boring part that actually matters.

Routing.

I run Claude Code agents across my entire GTM stack. Content generation, lead enrichment, CRM updates, SEO monitoring, deploy pipelines. The orchestration isn't the hard part. Deciding which agent gets which task, with which context, at which moment... that's where sessions fall apart.

I built a routing skill that sits in front of every agent invocation. It reads the task, checks constraints, decides: solo session, subagent, or full team. Three lines of logic that saved me from the thing that kills most multi-agent setups.

Context bleed.

When you throw everything into one agent context, you get drift. When you spin up too many subagents, you get duplication. The router keeps the main window clean and delegates research to throwaway contexts.

The pattern I keep coming back to: one task per subagent, research in parallel, synthesis in the main thread. It's not clever. It's just plumbing.

Which is maybe why it works.
posts.cta: If you're running multi-agent setups, what's your biggest failure mode? Mine was context bleed by a mile.

Sharing our internal architecture for chaining 5+ specialized subagents without context bleed — the key insight is treating each agent like a stateless function with a strict input/output contract. Most teams getting this wrong are passing too much context upstream.

remixes.label: tactical-breakdown
remixes.hook: I spent 3 weeks building agent orchestration. Then I spent 3 months fixing the routing layer underneath it.
remixes.body:
I spent 3 weeks building agent orchestration. Then I spent 3 months fixing the routing layer underneath it.

Here's what nobody warns you about multi-agent systems: the agents work fine in isolation. The disaster starts when you have to decide which one gets the job.

My content agent and my CRM agent both thought they owned lead data. My SEO agent was getting context meant for my deploy pipeline. I had agents fighting over shared state like toddlers over a toy.

The fix wasn't better agents. It was a routing skill. One file that reads the incoming task, checks what context is available, and assigns it to exactly one agent with exactly the context it needs. Nothing more.

Three rules that stopped the bleeding:

1. Every task gets classified before any agent sees it. No ambiguity.
2. Context is scoped per-agent. If the enrichment agent doesn't need CRM history, it doesn't get CRM history.
3. Fallback routing exists. If classification confidence is low, it goes to a general agent, not a specialist.

The orchestration layer I was so proud of? It's maybe 40 lines. The routing logic underneath it is 400. That ratio tells you everything about where the real complexity lives.
remixes.cta: What's the ratio of routing logic to orchestration logic in your agent setup? I bet it's more lopsided than you think.

remixes.label: contrarian-flip
remixes.hook: Multi-agent is not an architecture decision. It's a context management decision wearing a trench coat.
remixes.body:
Multi-agent is not an architecture decision. It's a context management decision wearing a trench coat.

I know this because I built the architecture first. Separate agents for content, enrichment, CRM, deploys. Clean boundaries. Beautiful diagram. Terrible results.

The problem was never "can these agents do their jobs." They could. The problem was that every task carries context, and context has weight. Send too much context and the agent drowns. Send too little and it hallucinates. Send the wrong shape and it confidently does the wrong thing.

So I stopped thinking about agents and started thinking about context packets. What does this specific task need? What would poison it? What's the minimum viable context window?

Now my "multi-agent system" is really a context router with agents attached. The router decides what information flows where. The agents are almost interchangeable.

This reframe changed everything. I stopped debugging agent behavior and started debugging context quality. Turns out most agent failures aren't agent failures. They're context failures that happen to manifest inside an agent.

The boring insight: if you get routing and context scoping right, you can use mediocre agents and still get great results. If you get them wrong, brilliant agents will produce garbage.
remixes.cta: Have you ever traced an agent failure back to a context problem? Once you start looking, it's almost always the root cause.

Routing is the critical layer most teams skip when building multi-agent systems. I've deployed Claude Code agents across content generation, lead enrichment, CRM updates, SEO monitoring, and deploy pipelines. The orchestration was straightforward. The routing was not.

Here's what I recommend focusing on first: task classification. Before any agent touches a task, a routing layer should determine which agent gets it, what context it receives, and what context gets excluded. Without this, you get context bleed, where Agent A's state leaks into Agent B's decision-making.

Three patterns I've seen work consistently:

First, explicit context scoping. Each agent gets a defined context boundary. No shared state unless deliberately passed through.

Second, confidence-based fallback. If the router can't classify a task with high confidence, it goes to a generalist agent rather than a specialist that might mishandle it.

Third, logging at the routing layer. Most teams log agent outputs. The higher-leverage move is logging routing decisions. When you can see why a task went to a specific agent with specific context, debugging becomes trivial.

The orchestration framework you choose matters far less than the routing logic you build underneath it. Start there.

posts.title: Stop measuring agent vibes
posts.hook: We evaluated our AI agents for 6 months by asking "does this look right?" That's not evaluation. That's hope.
posts.body:
We evaluated our AI agents for 6 months by asking "does this look right?" That's not evaluation. That's hope.

The shift happened when I started logging every agent output to SQLite. Not fancy. Just a table with task_id, input_hash, output, and a pass/fail column I'd fill in manually for the first few weeks.

After 200 rows I had enough signal to see the patterns. My enrichment agent was hallucinating company descriptions 11% of the time. My content agent was recycling the same hook structure in 40% of drafts. My CRM agent was silently dropping fields when the source data had unicode.

None of that showed up in "does this look right" spot checks.

The eval doesn't need to be a framework. It needs to be a table you actually look at. I query mine every morning:

SELECT task_type, COUNT(*) as total, SUM(CASE WHEN passed = 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) as failures FROM agent_evals WHERE date > date('now', '-7 days') GROUP BY task_type;

Seven lines of SQL replaced my gut feeling with a failure rate I can act on.

The agents didn't get better because I found a better model. They got better because I finally measured where they were broken.
posts.cta: What's your agent eval setup? Or are you still in the "looks good to me" phase? No judgment, I was there for months.

inspired_by.summary: We just open-sourced our internal agent evaluation harness. After 6 months of running production AI agents, we found MMLU and HumanEval completely useless for predicting real-world reliability. What actually matters: tool call accuracy under adversarial inputs, graceful degradation on ambiguous prompts, and cost-per-resolved-task. Link in comments.

remixes.label: build-log
remixes.hook: 200 rows in a SQLite table taught me more about my AI agents than 6 months of eyeballing outputs.
remixes.body:
200 rows in a SQLite table taught me more about my AI agents than 6 months of eyeballing outputs.

I was running an enrichment agent that pulled company data, matched contacts, and scored leads. It "looked right" most of the time. I'd spot-check a few results, nod, move on.

Then I started logging. Nothing fancy. A table: task_id, input_hash, output, pass_fail. For the first few weeks I manually reviewed every row and marked it pass or fail.

At row 200, the patterns were obvious.

My enrichment agent hallucinated company descriptions 23% of the time. Not made-up companies. Real companies with plausible but wrong descriptions. The kind of wrong that looks right if you're skimming.

My content agent front-loaded buzzwords in the first sentence 40% of the time, despite explicit instructions not to.

My CRM agent silently dropped fields when the input had more than 8 data points.

None of this was visible through spot-checking. It only showed up in aggregate.

The eval table took 10 minutes to create. The manual review took maybe 30 minutes a day for two weeks. The ROI on those hours was the highest of anything I've done with agents.

Now I have automated checks that catch 80% of these patterns. But the automated checks only exist because I did the manual work first.
remixes.cta: What's the first pattern you'd look for if you started logging agent outputs today?

remixes.label: framework-critique
remixes.hook: The AI industry is building evaluation frameworks. I built a spreadsheet. Mine works better.
remixes.body:
The AI industry is building evaluation frameworks. I built a spreadsheet. Mine works better.

Every week there's a new agent evaluation tool. Tracing platforms, LLM-as-judge pipelines, automated benchmark suites. I've tried several. They all share the same problem: they evaluate what the framework designers think matters, not what actually matters for your specific use case.

My enrichment agent doesn't need to pass a general benchmark. It needs to not hallucinate company descriptions. My content agent doesn't need a creativity score. It needs to stop front-loading buzzwords.

So I built the dumbest possible eval. SQLite table. Manual pass/fail for two weeks. Then I looked at the failures and wrote specific checks for the specific patterns I found.

Check 1: Does the company description match what's on their actual website? (Cross-reference with a simple web fetch.)
Check 2: Does the first sentence contain any word from my buzzword list?
Check 3: Did all input fields make it to the output?

Three checks. Caught 80% of the problems. Total infrastructure cost: zero. Total setup time: an afternoon.

The evaluation frameworks aren't wrong. They're premature. You need to understand your failure modes before you can evaluate against them. And understanding your failure modes requires the boring manual work that no framework can skip.
remixes.cta: Are you evaluating against your actual failure modes, or against someone else's benchmark?

posts.title: AI-native tools vs. AI-augmented tools
posts.hook: There are two kinds of dev tools being built right now. One assumes you can code. The other assumes you can't. Both are right.
posts.body:
There are two kinds of dev tools being built right now. One assumes you can code. The other assumes you can't. Both are right.

I use Claude Code as my primary development environment. It assumes I understand what's happening. I set constraints, review diffs, manage context windows. The agent does the typing but I'm steering.

Then I watch founders who've never written a line ship full SaaS products with cursor-style tools that abstract the code away entirely.

Both approaches work. But they produce very different systems.

The AI-native path (code optional) optimizes for speed to first version. The AI-augmented path (code required) optimizes for systems you can debug at 2am when something breaks in production.

I'm biased toward the second camp because my stack runs 24/7. Cron jobs, webhooks, data pipelines, deploy hooks. When the enrichment agent silently starts returning empty arrays at midnight, I need to read the code to fix it.

The bifurcation isn't about skill level. It's about what happens after you ship.

If your product is a landing page and a Stripe link, the no-code AI path is genuinely better. If your product IS the system... you need to be able to read it.
posts.cta: Where do you fall? Building with AI as a copilot, or building with AI as the pilot?

inspired_by.author: Cassidy Williams
inspired_by.summary: Hot take: the developer tool landscape in 2026 is bifurcating hard. One camp is building AI-native tools that assume your agent writes the code. The other is still bolting Copilot onto legacy IDEs. The gap between these two camps is going to be wider than the gap between mobile-first and desktop-first was in 2012. If your DevEx stack isn't agent-native, you're already behind.

remixes.label: spectrum-model
remixes.hook: The debate between "AI copilot" and "AI autopilot" misses the point. It's not a binary. It's a slider, and you should be moving it constantly.
remixes.body:
The debate between "AI copilot" and "AI autopilot" misses the point. It's not a binary. It's a slider, and you should be moving it constantly.

Some days I'm deep in Claude Code, reviewing every diff, managing context windows, steering architecture decisions. Full copilot mode. The agent types, I think.

Other days I point an agent at a well-defined task, walk away, and come back to a finished result. Full autopilot mode. I defined the constraints upfront and let it run.

The skill isn't picking one mode. It's knowing which mode fits the task.

Architectural decisions? Copilot. I need to think through tradeoffs.
Boilerplate CRUD endpoints? Autopilot. The constraints are obvious.
Bug investigation? Copilot. I need to understand root cause.
Test generation from existing specs? Autopilot. Mechanical transformation.

Most people pick a mode and stick with it. The "I review everything" crowd spends hours watching agents write boilerplate. The "AI does everything" crowd ships bugs in their architecture.

The leverage comes from switching fluidly. High oversight for high-stakes decisions. Low oversight for well-constrained tasks. The ratio shifts as you build trust with your tools and as the tools get better.

I'd estimate I'm in copilot mode 40% of the time now. Six months ago it was 90%. Six months from now it might be 20%. The slider only moves in one direction.
remixes.cta: What's your copilot-to-autopilot ratio right now? And is it shifting?

remixes.label: founder-paradox
remixes.hook: A founder who can't code just shipped a production app in 3 days. A senior engineer took 2 weeks on a similar scope. Both made the right call.
remixes.body:
A founder who can't code just shipped a production app in 3 days. A senior engineer took 2 weeks on a similar scope. Both made the right call.

The founder used Cursor and v0. Described what they wanted in plain English. The AI generated everything. They shipped, got users, started iterating. They don't understand their own codebase. They don't need to yet.

The engineer used Claude Code. Reviewed every architectural decision. Chose the database schema carefully. Set up proper error handling, testing, CI/CD. They understand every line. They'll iterate faster at scale.

Neither approach is wrong because they're solving different problems.

The founder is validating a market. Speed to feedback is everything. Technical debt is irrelevant if nobody wants the product. The AI-as-pilot approach is perfect here.

The engineer is building for durability. They know this product has users. They need it to scale, to be maintainable, to handle edge cases. The AI-as-copilot approach is perfect here.

The mistake is using one approach for both situations. Founders who over-engineer before validation waste time. Engineers who ship without understanding create time bombs.

The tools are the same. The judgment about which mode to use is the actual skill. And that judgment has nothing to do with whether you can code.
remixes.cta: When was the last time you deliberately chose a different level of AI involvement based on what the task actually needed?

posts.title: Agent infra Cambrian explosion
posts.hook: Every week there's a new AI agent infrastructure company. Vector DB, memory layer, orchestration framework, observability platform. I use SQLite for all four.
posts.body:
Every week there's a new AI agent infrastructure company. Vector DB, memory layer, orchestration framework, observability platform. I use SQLite for all four.

Not because I'm against infrastructure. Because most agent infra is solving problems you don't have yet.

My memory layer is a table called memory_fts with full-text search. My orchestration is a routing skill that reads a task and picks solo vs. subagent. My observability is a daily_costs table I query every morning. My vector search is grep.

This runs a production GTM system. Enrichment, outreach, content, CRM sync, SEO tracking. All on one Mac Mini.

The Cambrian explosion in agent infra reminds me of the martech explosion from 2018. 8,000 tools on a landscape slide. Most companies needed 4 of them.

The pattern repeats: infrastructure companies launch, raise funding, build features for enterprise edge cases, and then solo operators realize they can get 90% of the value from a database file and a cron job.

I'm not saying don't use agent infra. I'm saying build without it first. You'll know exactly which piece you actually need when you hit a wall that SQLite can't solve.

I haven't hit that wall yet.
posts.cta: What agent infra are you actually using in production vs. what you signed up for and never configured?

My entire agent infrastructure is one SQLite database. Not because I'm cheap. Because every tool I tried solved a problem I didn't actually have.

I signed up for three vector databases last year. Configured one. Used it for two weeks. Realized my use case was full-text search, not semantic similarity. Switched to SQLite FTS5. Faster, simpler, zero infrastructure to manage.

I evaluated four orchestration frameworks. Built a prototype with one. Realized my "orchestration" was a routing function that reads a task and picks an agent. It's a case statement. It doesn't need a framework.

I trialed two observability platforms. Set up dashboards, configured alerts. Realized I was looking at the same three metrics I could get from a SQL query against my logs table.

Here's what I actually use in production:

- memory_fts table: full-text search over agent memory. 50 lines of schema.
- routing skill: reads task, picks agent, scopes context. One markdown file.
- logs table: every agent run with input, output, duration, pass/fail. Basic SQL for reporting.
- secrets table: API keys and config. Key-value store.

All of it lives in one .db file. Backs up with a file copy. Migrates by opening it on a new machine.

I'm not saying infrastructure tools are bad. I'm saying most of them are premature for most agent deployments. Build with the simplest thing that works. Add infrastructure when you hit a real wall, not a hypothetical one.
remixes.cta: What's the most overengineered part of your agent setup? The thing that could be replaced with a simpler approach?

remixes.label: vendor-trap

remixes.body:
Agent infrastructure companies need you to believe your problem is complex. It usually isn't.

I've been watching the agent tooling space for a year. The pattern is consistent: take a simple concept, add a managed service around it, price it per API call, and market it as essential.

Vector database? Most agent use cases need keyword search, not semantic similarity. SQLite FTS5 handles it.

Memory layer? It's a table. Key, value, timestamp, maybe a category column. You don't need a platform for this.

Orchestration framework? If you have more than 5 agents, maybe. If you have 2-3, it's a routing function. A switch statement with context scoping.

Observability platform? Log your agent runs to a table. Query it with SQL. You'll get the same insights without a monthly bill.

I'm not against these tools existing. Some teams genuinely need them at scale. But the marketing creates artificial complexity anxiety. You see the enterprise-grade dashboard and think "I should have that." You probably shouldn't. Not yet.

The test I use: can I solve this with a SQLite table and a Python script? If yes, I do that first. If I hit a genuine scaling wall, then I evaluate tools. I've been running this way for months. Haven't hit the wall yet.

The agent infra Cambrian explosion will consolidate. Most of these companies will die. The ones that survive will serve genuinely complex use cases. Yours probably isn't one of them yet.
remixes.cta: What agent tool did you sign up for, configure halfway, and quietly abandon? We've all got at least one.

posts.title: Signal quality over activity volume
posts.hook: I used to track emails sent. Now I track signals consumed. The difference in pipeline quality is embarrassing.
posts.body:
I used to track emails sent. Now I track signals consumed. The difference in pipeline quality is embarrassing.

Old dashboard: 847 emails sent this week, 12% open rate, 2% reply rate. Felt productive. Pipeline was mid.

New dashboard: 23 intent signals detected, 14 qualified, 9 sequences triggered. Feels slow. Pipeline is 3x better.

The shift: I built a signal layer that watches for job posts mentioning tools in our space, Reddit threads asking about problems we solve, and funding announcements in our ICP. Each signal gets scored and only triggers outreach if it crosses a threshold.

The scoring is simple. Three fields: recency (days since signal), relevance (keyword match count), and reach (company size bucket). Weights in a JSON config I tune monthly.

Most outbound teams are still optimizing for volume because that's what the tooling measures. Send more, dial more, book more. But when you flip to signal-first, you realize half your sequences were going to accounts with zero buying intent.

The uncomfortable math: 23 signal-triggered emails at a 35% reply rate produce more pipeline than 847 spray-and-pray emails at 2%.

Same human. Same offer. Different input.
posts.cta: What signals are you actually tracking before triggering outreach? Or is it still list --> sequence --> pray?

remixes.label: pipeline-autopsy
remixes.hook: I deleted our outbound dashboard and rebuilt it from scratch. The old one measured effort. The new one measures signal quality. Pipeline tripled.
remixes.body:
I deleted our outbound dashboard and rebuilt it from scratch. The old one measured effort. The new one measures signal quality. Pipeline tripled.

Old dashboard had the classics: emails sent, open rate, reply rate, meetings booked. All activity metrics. They made us feel productive. They were lying to us.

847 emails sent in a week. 12% open rate. 2% reply rate. Looks like a functioning outbound motion, right? The pipeline from those emails was mediocre. Low conversion, high churn, poor fit.

New dashboard has five metrics:

1. Intent signals detected (job posts, tech stack changes, funding events)
2. Signals qualified (matched against our ICP)
3. Sequences triggered (only fired on qualified signals)
4. Signal-to-meeting ratio
5. Signal-sourced pipeline value

The volume dropped dramatically. 847 emails became 9 targeted sequences. But those 9 sequences produced 3x the pipeline of the 847.

The insight isn't that signals are better than spray-and-pray. Everyone says that. The insight is that activity metrics actively hide bad pipeline quality. When your dashboard shows 847 emails sent, it feels like progress. It's not. It's noise that makes it impossible to see the signal.

I had to remove the activity metrics entirely to see the truth. Not add signal metrics alongside them. Remove the old ones. Because as long as the volume numbers were visible, they created a false sense of productivity that prevented honest evaluation.
remixes.cta: What metric on your current dashboard gives you a false sense of progress? The one that would hurt to remove but might be hiding the truth.

remixes.label: signal-stack
remixes.hook: My outbound team sends fewer emails than ever. Pipeline has never been better. Here's the signal layer that made the difference.
remixes.body:
My outbound team sends fewer emails than ever. Pipeline has never been better. Here's the signal layer that made the difference.

We built a system that watches for three categories of signals before any outreach gets triggered:

Hiring signals: Job posts that mention our category. If a company is hiring for a role that uses tools we replace or augment, that's intent. Not "they might be interested" intent. "They're actively investing in this problem" intent.

Tech stack signals: Changes detected through public data. New integrations mentioned on their site, job posts requiring specific tools, case studies referencing technology shifts. These tell you a company is in motion.

Timing signals: Funding rounds, leadership changes, product launches. These create windows where companies are more open to new approaches.

Each signal gets scored. A hiring signal alone is moderate intent. A hiring signal plus a tech stack change is strong. All three together is urgent.

The scoring determines the sequence. Moderate intent gets a softer, educational approach. Strong intent gets direct. Urgent intent gets a phone call.

Before this system, we treated every prospect the same. Same sequence, same cadence, same message. The signal layer made our outreach feel personalized without manually personalizing each message. The context was already embedded in the routing.

23 signals detected last week. 14 qualified. 9 sequences triggered. Better pipeline than months of volume-based outbound.
remixes.cta: Which signal type would be most valuable for your specific ICP? Hiring, tech stack, or timing? The answer depends on your sales cycle.

posts.title: GTM engineering is a forcing function
posts.hook: GTM engineering isn't a job title you hire for. It's what happens when one person gets tired of waiting on three teams.
posts.body:
GTM engineering isn't a job title you hire for. It's what happens when one person gets tired of waiting on three teams.

I needed enriched company data for outbound. Marketing said Q3. RevOps said backlog. Engineering said "file a ticket."

So I wrote a Python script that hits the Clearbit API, stores results in SQLite, and pushes qualified accounts to Attio. Took an afternoon.

That script replaced a workflow that previously required a Clay table ($$$), an ops person to maintain it, and a 2-week lag between signal and outreach.

This is the pattern I keep seeing. GTM engineering emerges when the gap between "what I need" and "what the stack provides" gets wide enough that building is faster than requesting.

It's not about replacing SDRs. It's about removing the bottlenecks that make SDRs waste half their day on data hygiene instead of conversations.

The forcing function part: once you build one piece yourself, you see how much of your GTM stack is duct tape and manual steps. Then you build the next piece. Then the next.

Six months later you have a system that runs while you sleep and you're wondering why you ever paid five figures for tools that did less.
posts.cta: What was the first GTM workflow you automated yourself? That first one always changes how you see the rest of the stack.

remixes.label: bottleneck-bypass
remixes.hook: Every GTM bottleneck I've hit in the last year had the same root cause: waiting for someone else to prioritize my pipeline.
remixes.body:
Every GTM bottleneck I've hit in the last year had the same root cause: waiting for someone else to prioritize my pipeline.

Marketing has their own roadmap. Engineering has their own sprint. RevOps has 14 other requests ahead of yours. Nobody is being unreasonable. They just don't feel the same pain you feel when deals stall because your enrichment data is three weeks stale.

So you learn enough Python to be dangerous. You string together an API, a database, and a CRM webhook. It's not pretty. It works.

That's the moment GTM engineering starts. Not when someone posts the job description. When someone decides the cost of waiting exceeds the cost of learning.

I've watched this pattern repeat across a dozen founders and operators. The first script is always ugly. The second one has error handling. By the third, they've built a system that would take a cross-functional team two quarters to spec out.

The irony is that the people best positioned to do this are the ones closest to revenue. They know which data matters because they've lost deals without it.
remixes.cta: What's the GTM bottleneck you stopped waiting on and just solved yourself? Those stories are more useful than any tool review.

remixes.label: accidental-engineer
remixes.hook: I didn't set out to become a GTM engineer. I set out to close a deal and nobody could get me the data fast enough.
remixes.body:
I didn't set out to become a GTM engineer. I set out to close a deal and nobody could get me the data fast enough.

The deal needed firmographic data we didn't have. Our enrichment tool was rate-limited. Marketing owned the vendor contract. RevOps was mid-migration. I had 72 hours before the prospect went dark.

So I opened a terminal. Wrote 40 lines of Python. Hit an API. Got the data. Pushed it into our CRM. Sent the follow-up.

Deal closed.

Nobody asked me how I got the data. Nobody cared that I bypassed the official workflow. They cared that pipeline moved forward.

This is how most GTM engineering actually starts. Not with a mandate from leadership. Not with a headcount req. With one person who needed something done Tuesday, not next quarter.

The skill gap between 'can operate a CRM' and 'can build on top of a CRM' is smaller than people think. A weekend with an API doc and a scripting language gets you further than six months on a vendor waitlist.

The people doing this work don't call themselves engineers. They call themselves 'tired of waiting.'
remixes.cta: If you've hacked together a GTM workflow out of frustration, I want to hear about it. Those builds are usually the ones that stick.

posts.title: Writing for buyers not algorithms
posts.hook: Our best-performing content last quarter had zero SEO optimization. It just answered a question a buyer actually asked on a sales call.
posts.body:
Our best-performing content last quarter had zero SEO optimization. It just answered a question a buyer actually asked on a sales call.

The post was about how to evaluate whether you need a Clay table or a custom script. No keyword research. No header optimization. No internal linking strategy. Just a straight answer to "when does Clay stop making sense?"

It got picked up by three newsletters, drove 40+ inbound profile views, and started 6 conversations that turned into pipeline.

Meanwhile, the SEO-optimized comparison post we spent a week on? Ranked page 2. Zero conversations.

The algorithm-first trap is real. You write for crawlers, structure for featured snippets, optimize for keywords your buyer never actually searches. The content technically performs. It ranks, it gets impressions, it looks good in the monthly report.

But it doesn't start conversations. And conversations are where pipeline comes from.

I flipped my content process. Every Monday I review the last 5 sales calls and pull out the questions that came up more than once. Those become posts. No keyword tool involved.

The irony: content written for actual buyers tends to rank anyway, because it matches the way people actually search... in full questions, not keyword fragments.
posts.cta: Pull up your last 3 sales calls. What questions kept coming up? That's your content calendar.

inspired_by.author: Melissa Rosenthal
inspired_by.summary: Hot take: your content strategy is failing because your marketing team is writing for the algorithm instead of the buyer. I reviewed 60 LinkedIn company pages last week. Every single one led with features, not problems. Buyers don't care what your product does. They care about what breaks when they don't have it. Content that converts starts with the pain, not the pitch — and most teams have this completely backwards.

remixes.label: sales-call-content-mine
remixes.hook: Your content team is brainstorming topics in a conference room. Meanwhile, your sales team is hearing the exact topics buyers care about on every call.
remixes.body:
Your content team is brainstorming topics in a conference room. Meanwhile, your sales team is hearing the exact topics buyers care about on every call.

I started recording the questions prospects ask during discovery calls. Not the objections. The genuine 'I don't know how to think about this' questions.

Things like: 'When should I stop using Clay and write a custom script?' or 'How do I know if my enrichment vendor is actually giving me good data?'

These aren't keyword targets. They're real confusion from people actively trying to buy something. They just need someone to explain it clearly.

I wrote a blog post answering one of these questions. No SEO research. No keyword density. No competitive analysis. Just a direct answer to a real question.

Three newsletters picked it up. It drove more qualified traffic than anything our SEO-optimized content produced that quarter.

The lesson isn't that SEO is bad. It's that most content strategies start with what Google wants instead of what buyers need. Flip the order. Start with the sales call. Write the answer. Let SEO catch up later.

Buyers don't search in keywords. They search in questions. Your sales team hears those questions every day.

We stopped optimizing content for search and our organic traffic went up. Here's what actually happened.

For six months, we followed the playbook. Keyword research, header optimization, internal linking, meta descriptions. We published 12 posts. They ranked. They got traffic. They generated almost zero pipeline.

posts.title: CRM data graveyard
posts.hook: Ran a query on our CRM last week. 62% of contact records had no activity in 90+ days. Leadership was using those records in their forecast.
posts.body:
Ran a query on our CRM last week. 62% of contact records had no activity in 90+ days. Leadership was using those records in their forecast.

This is the quiet crisis in RevOps. The CRM looks full. Dashboards look healthy. Forecasts look reasonable. But the underlying data is a graveyard of stale contacts, outdated titles, and companies that pivoted 6 months ago.

I built a decay score. Simple concept: every contact starts at 100. Loses 5 points per week with no activity. Gains points for replies, site visits, or signal matches. Anything below 30 gets flagged.

The results were painful. Over half our "active pipeline" was contacts who hadn't engaged since initial outreach. We were forecasting revenue against ghosts.

The fix wasn't more data entry discipline. People don't update CRMs. That's not a training problem, it's a design problem.

The fix was automation. A nightly script that checks engagement signals, updates decay scores, and moves stale records to a quarantine stage. If a contact re-engages, they automatically get restored.

Forecasting accuracy went from "leadership guesses" to something I'd actually trust within 6 weeks.

Your CRM isn't dirty because your team is lazy. It's dirty because manual data maintenance doesn't scale.

posts.title: Weekend build to 10k MRR
posts.hook: The gap between "built in a weekend" and "$10k MRR" is not the build. It's the 6 months of distribution nobody screenshots.
posts.body:
The gap between "built in a weekend" and "$10k MRR" is not the build. It's the 6 months of distribution nobody screenshots.

I see these posts every week. "Built this tool in 48 hours, just hit $10k MRR." The screenshot shows the Stripe dashboard. What it doesn't show: the 200 Reddit comments, the 50 cold DMs to early users, the 3 pivots on positioning, the pricing page they rewrote 4 times.

I've shipped tools in a weekend too. Claude Code makes the build trivial. You can go from idea to deployed product in a day if the scope is tight enough.

But getting 47 paying customers? That's a distribution problem. And distribution is a grind that doesn't compress the way code does.

The founders I watch succeed at this aren't better builders. They're better at finding the 5 communities where their buyer already hangs out and showing up there consistently for months.

My own pattern: I built Clearbox's first version fast. Getting the first paying users took 10x longer than the build. Reddit threads, LinkedIn posts, direct outreach to people who matched the ICP. One conversation at a time.

The weekend build is the easy part. The Monday after is where the work starts.
posts.cta: What's your distribution channel that actually works? Not the one you wish worked. The one that brings paying users.

Every "built it in a weekend" story has 6 months of distribution work hiding below the surface. The screenshot shows Stripe. It doesn't show the 200 Reddit comments.

I've been building tools for two years. The build is never the bottleneck. Getting people to care is the bottleneck.

Here's what the timeline actually looks like for most solo products that hit $10k MRR:

Week 1: Build the thing. It works. You're excited.
Weeks 2 through 8: Post about it everywhere. Nobody cares. You wonder if the product is wrong.
Weeks 9 through 16: Find one distribution channel that gets traction. Double down. Rewrite your positioning twice.
Weeks 17 through 24: Revenue starts compounding. You rewrite the pricing page. You add the feature that three paying users asked for. Growth stabilizes.

That's the real story. But the post that gets engagement is the screenshot with the Stripe graph going up and a one-liner about building it in a weekend.

I'm not saying those posts are dishonest. The build probably did take a weekend. But the build was maybe 5% of getting to $10k. The other 95% is the grind of finding people who want it and convincing them to pay.

Distribution is the product. The code is just the thing being distributed.
remixes.cta: What's the distribution channel that actually works for you? Not the one you post about. The one that brings paying users.

Shipping a product takes a weekend. Selling it takes six months. The gap between those two timelines is where most solo projects die.

The build-in-public community has a narrative problem. The stories that get engagement are the compressed ones. "Built this in 48 hours, just hit $10k MRR." Stripe screenshot. Rocket emoji. Thousands of likes.

What's missing from the story: the 50 cold DMs to early users who mostly ignored them. The three positioning pivots when the original landing page converted at 0.2%. The pricing page rewritten four times. The Reddit threads where they gave away the product for free just to get feedback.

I've shipped a dozen side projects. The ones that made money all had the same shape: fast build, slow distribution, eventual product-market fit through repetition and stubbornness.

The ones that failed also had the same shape: fast build, assumed distribution would be organic, waited for traffic that never came.

The difference was never the product. It was whether I had a distribution channel I could work consistently for months. Not virality. Not a lucky HN post. A channel I could show up to every day and push.

If you're planning a weekend build, spend the first hour planning distribution. Where will you find the first 10 users? If you can't answer that, the weekend build doesn't matter.

posts.hook: I've shipped more production code in the last 30 days than I did in my first year of learning to code. The difference isn't skill. It's the loop.

I've shipped more production code in the last 30 days than I did in my first year of learning to code. The difference isn't skill. It's the loop.

My development loop with Claude Code:

1. Write a plan in markdown. Constraints, inputs, outputs, edge cases.
2. Hand the plan to the agent. It builds. I review diffs.
3. Run the build. If it breaks, paste the error back. Agent fixes.
4. Ship. Write a context handoff doc so the next session picks up clean.

That's it. No IDE. No Stack Overflow. No 3-hour debugging sessions where I'm guessing at syntax.

The context handoff is the part most people skip and it's the most important piece. Every session ends with a markdown doc: what was built, what's pending, what broke, what to try next. The next session reads it and starts warm.

Without handoffs, every session starts cold and you waste 20 minutes re-explaining your codebase. With handoffs, session two picks up mid-thought.

I'm not a developer by training. I was a plumber for 10 years. But the loop... plan, build, review, handoff... that's just project management. Same pattern whether you're running pipe or running code.

The tool changed. The discipline didn't.

The most important file in my codebase isn't code. It's a markdown file that tells the AI what happened yesterday.

When I start the next session, the agent reads that file first. It doesn't ask me what we were working on. It doesn't rebuild context from scratch. It picks up where we left off.

Before I started doing this, every session started with 10 minutes of re-explaining. The agent would suggest approaches I'd already tried. It would miss constraints I'd discovered the day before. It would re-introduce bugs I'd already fixed.

The handoff document eliminated all of that. Five minutes of writing saves 30 minutes of context rebuilding.

But here's what surprised me: the handoffs also made me a better developer. Writing down what happened, what worked, and what failed forces clarity. I catch my own bad decisions while documenting them. I notice patterns I missed during implementation.

The loop isn't human tells AI what to build. It's human writes context, AI builds, human reviews, human writes better context. Each cycle tightens.

I've shipped more production code in 30 days with this loop than I did in my first year of learning to code. The model didn't get smarter. My context got better.
